title: Best Webcams UK
short: Webcams compared by image quality, low-light performance and features, from budget picks to 4K streaming cameras.
intro: Higher resolution doesn't automatically mean a better picture, since most video calling apps cap out at 1080p anyway. This guide compares webcams tested by Tom's Hardware across identical well-lit, low-light and overexposed lighting scenarios, from budget picks to 4K streaming cameras.

products.name: Brio 500
products.best_for: Most people upgrading from a laptop's built-in camera
products.summary: Tom's Hardware's pick for most people. Despite a modest 1080p/30fps spec, its flexible 90-degree field of view and 'RightLight 4' processing give an impressively exposure-balanced image out of the box, with auto-white balance nearly matching much pricier webcams.

products.name: Link
products.best_for: Creators who move around or present and want AI tracking
products.key_spec: 4K/30fps on a 3-axis gimbal, AI movement tracking
products.summary: An AI-powered 4K webcam mounted on its own 3-axis gimbal, with some of the best auto-exposure, colour reproduction and autofocus Tom's Hardware has seen on a webcam. Powerful for presenters or creators who move a lot, though overkill and expensive for average video calls.
pros: AI-powered movement tracking and capture modes

products.name: Facecam Neo
products.best_for: Buyers who just need a solid, affordable upgrade
products.summary: A simple, plug-and-play budget webcam that performed impressively well in Tom's Hardware's low-light test, with a physical privacy shutter and a permanently attached braided USB-C cable, though the picture can look a little blown out and it lacks a built-in mic.
cons: Picture can look blown out in bright scenes

products.name: YoloCam S3
products.best_for: Streamers and content creators who want 4K on a budget
products.summary: A small, sturdy 4K webcam with a large sensor for its class and a crisp, clear picture with decent auto-exposure and white balance across all of Tom's Hardware's lighting tests. Includes a magnetic monitor mount and detailed colour-grading software, but has no built-in privacy shutter or lens cap.
cons: No lens cap or privacy shutter

products.name: Kiyo Pro Ultra
products.best_for: Buyers who want the sharpest, most film-like image
products.summary: The largest sensor Tom's Hardware has seen in a webcam, giving excellent auto-exposure, colour balancing and a shallow depth-of-field that blurs the background without software. Image quality is shockingly good even against other 4K webcams, though the Synapse 3 software is frustrating to use alongside other apps.
cons: Razer Synapse app is frustrating to use

products.name: Pro Webcam (WB5023)
products.best_for: Buyers who want more than 1080p without paying for 4K
products.summary: A good middle ground for buyers who want extra resolution for zooming and cropping without a 4K price. Performs well in all lighting scenarios right out of the box and is especially strong in low light, though auto-white balance runs a little sallow and the built-in mic is weak.
cons: Auto-white balance runs a little sallow

guide.a: Probably not for video calls. Most conferencing apps like Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams cap streaming resolution at 1080p regardless of your webcam. A 4K webcam mainly helps if you plan to zoom and crop your feed, or you're recording or streaming content where the extra detail is actually visible.

guide.q: How much does low-light performance matter?
guide.a: A lot, for most home setups. Few home offices have studio lighting, so a webcam that handles low light and mixed lighting well, like the Logitech Brio 500 or Elgato Facecam Neo here, will look noticeably better in everyday use than one that only looks good under bright, even light.

guide.q: Should I use the webcam's built-in microphone?
guide.a: Generally, no. Even webcams with a 'good' built-in mic, like the Logitech Brio 500, still capture more room echo and background noise than a dedicated USB microphone or headset. If sound quality matters for your calls, use a separate microphone.

guide.q: Is a physical privacy shutter important?
guide.a: It's a simple, reliable way to guarantee your camera isn't capturing video, without relying on software settings. If privacy matters to you, it's worth prioritising a model with a built-in physical shutter, like the Facecam Neo or Kiyo Pro Ultra here, over one that requires a separate cap.
